bibauthors evaluation set
========================

Two hand-labelled fixture sets and what they are for.

  name_pairs.json   154 name pairs, labelled "same" or "different"
  entries.json       27 bibliography entries, labelled with a verdict

Both files are pure ASCII. Every character outside the printable ASCII range
is written as a JSON \uXXXX escape, so the files can be read, diffed and
grepped on a cp1252 console without an encoding step.

The harness that consumes them is tests/test_accuracy.py. The script that
prints the tables is tools/evaluate.py.


1. HOW THE LABELS WERE SET
--------------------------

The labels answer questions about the world, not about the code:

  name_pairs.json   do these two strings denote the same human being?
  entries.json      is the author list in this entry the real author list of
                    the work it claims to cite, and which of the seven
                    verdicts in src/bibauthors/verdict.py describes it?

Every label was written down before any part of bibauthors was run over the
set, and no label was changed afterwards because the tool disagreed. Where
the tool and the label disagree, the disagreement is reported as a result:
see sections 4 and 6 of tools/evaluate.py, and the KNOWN_PAIR_FAILURES and
KNOWN_ENTRY_FAILURES tables in tests/test_accuracy.py, which list all 26
failing pairs and both failing entries with the rule in names.py that
produced each answer.

No file under src/ was modified to produce these numbers. The numbers
describe the code as it was found.


2. PROVENANCE
-------------

Nothing in either set was scraped, generated by a model, or copied from
another citation-checking project.

Real people and real works. Most rows are built from the author lists of six
real works whose records are already committed under tests/fixtures/cache,
so the ground truth is a publisher deposit or an arXiv submission rather than
anybody's recollection:

  arXiv 2507.01413   Evaluating LLM Agent Collusion in Double Auctions
                     true authors: Kushal Agrawal, Verona Teo,
                     Juan J. Vazquez, Sudarsh Kunnavakkam, Vishak Srikanth,
                     Andy Liu
  arXiv 2412.15115   Qwen2.5 Technical Report (45 author entries, the first
                     two of which are the corporate tokens "Qwen" and ":")
  10.1038/nature16961              AlphaGo, 20 authors, one Dutch particle
                                   surname (van den Driessche)
  10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2       AlphaFold, 34 authors, one name with two
                                   diacritics (Zidek, U+017D U+00ED)
  10.1109/CVPR.2016.90             ResNet, 4 romanised Chinese names
  10.1103/PhysRevLett.116.061102   GW150914, 1012 author entries, of which
                                   one is a collaboration group object
  CrossRef bibliographic search    Attention Is All You Need, 8 authors

Public figures. A small number of pairs use well known people where the
ground truth is a matter of public record and does not depend on any
judgement of ours: George W. Bush against George H. W. Bush (father and
son), Michael I. Jordan against Michael B. Jordan (the Berkeley professor and
the actor), Dale Earnhardt Jr. against Dale Earnhardt Sr., Lev Tolstoy
against Leo Tolstoy, Pyotr Tchaikovsky against Pyotr Chaikovsky.

Invented names. The fabricated author lists in entries.json, and the
placeholder people in a few pair rows (Alice M. Carter, John Q. Smith), are
invented. They are invented deliberately and they are plausible on purpose: a
fabricated citation is made of plausible names, so a negative set made of
implausible ones measures nothing. None of the invented names was chosen to
resemble a real person, and none is attached to a real work except in the
entries that exist precisely to test a fabricated author list against a real
identifier.

Near-miss surnames. The twelve near_miss_surname pairs are pairs of real,
distinct, separately attested surnames that differ by one or two characters:
Agrawal / Aggarwal, Smith / Smyth, Chen / Chan, Johnson / Johnsen,
Petersen / Pedersen, Reyes / Reyez, Shah / Sha, Mehta / Mehra, Kaur / Kaul,
Nguyen / Nguyan, Silver / Silvers, Vinyals / Vinals. All twelve are labelled
"different". Several of them belong to real authors of the works above (Stig
Petersen and Oriol Vinyals are AlphaFold authors; David Silver is an AlphaGo
author; Kushal Agrawal is the first author of arXiv 2507.01413).

Overlap with the existing suite. tests/test_names.py already parametrises a
set of same-person and different-person pairs. This set was written
independently and is not a copy of it; where a case is genuinely the same
case (initials against a full given name, for instance) it appears in both,
because the point of the evaluation set is coverage of the real world rather
than novelty relative to the unit tests. The evaluation set is roughly three
times the size, it carries a ground-truth label rather than an expected
score, it groups rows into categories so the per-category table means
something, and it keeps its failures instead of only its passes.


3. COMPOSITION OF name_pairs.json
---------------------------------

154 pairs. 89 labelled "same" (57.8 per cent), 65 labelled "different"
(42.2 per cent).

  category                        n   same   different
  ------------------------------------------------------
  apostrophe                      6      4           2
  cjk_order                       8      5           3
  cjk_script                      6      4           2
  comma_order                     6      5           1
  diacritics                      8      7           1
  different_person               12      0          12
  exact                           6      6           0
  group                           8      5           3
  hyphenated                      8      6           2
  initial_collision              10      7           3
  initials                       10      9           1
  mc_mac                          6      3           3
  middle_initial_conflict         6      2           4
  middle_name                     8      8           0
  near_miss_surname              12      0          12
  particle                       10      8           2
  same_surname_different_person  10      0          10
  suffix                          6      3           3
  transliteration                 8      7           1
  ------------------------------------------------------
  19 categories                 154     89          65

The "different" half is deliberately hard. 34 of the 65 negatives are in the
three categories built from real, confusable people and surnames
(near_miss_surname, different_person, same_surname_different_person), and the
rest are structural traps: a particle swapped (van der / van den), a
generation suffix swapped (Jr. / Sr.), a Mc spelling against a Mac spelling,
an initial that contradicts a written given name. There are no easy negatives
of the "Smith against Nakamura" kind, because a set of those produces a
flattering number and tells nobody anything.

Each row carries a "note" that states why the label is what it is. The notes
are part of the data: they are what makes a disagreement arguable rather than
mysterious.


4. THE initial_collision QUESTION, AND THE POSITION THIS SET TAKES
------------------------------------------------------------------

The problem. When only an initial is available, the same string denotes
different people in different bibliographies. "J. Smith" is John Smith in one
reference list and Jane Smith in another. Asking "is J. Smith the same human
being as John Smith?" has no answer in the abstract.

The position taken here, applied consistently across all ten
initial_collision rows and everywhere else an initial meets a written given
name:

    An initial is a wildcard constrained to its letter. A pair is labelled
    "same" when the two spellings are CONSISTENT, that is, when there exists
    one human being that both spellings could denote. It is labelled
    "different" only when the two spellings CONTRADICT each other.

So "J. Smith" against "John Smith" is "same" (coll-01), and "J. Smith"
against "Jane Smith" is also "same" (coll-02), while "J. Smith" against
"Robert Smith" is "different" (coll-03) because J contradicts R.

Note what that implies. coll-01 and coll-02 cannot both be the same human,
and the set knows it: consistency is not a transitive relation, and this
labelling makes no claim that it is. The relation being labelled is
"compatible with", not "identical to".

Why this position and not the stricter one. The tool exists to tell a
researcher that a citation's author list does not belong to the work it cites,
which is an accusation of fabrication in all but name. The cost of being
wrong is asymmetric and the asymmetry is encoded in the tool's own defaults
(see the module docstring of src/bibauthors/verdict.py). Abbreviating given
names to initials is not a defect in a bibliography, it is what numeric and
many author-year styles require; a very large share of real .bib files carry
nothing else. A checker that treats "J. Smith" against "John Smith" as a
mismatch would fire on a large fraction of correctly written bibliographies,
and it would be guessing when it did, because it has no evidence that the
two are different. Under the stricter position the honest label for most of
these rows would be "unknown", and an evaluation set with an "unknown" class
would let the tool score well by never committing.

The consequence for the numbers, stated plainly. This position inflates the
measured recall, because it turns genuinely ambiguous rows into positives
that an initials-tolerant matcher gets right. It is the right position for
this tool, and it is the reason the per-category table exists: the
initial_collision rows are isolated so that anyone who prefers the stricter
reading can recompute without them. For reference, all ten
initial_collision rows currently agree with the tool, so dropping the
category entirely would move overall accuracy from 128/154 to 118/144, which
is 0.8311 to 0.8194, and would move recall from 83/89 to 76/82, which is
0.9326 to 0.9268.


5. COMPOSITION OF entries.json
------------------------------

27 entries, every one of them resolvable offline against tests/fixtures/cache
(the two UNVERIFIABLE entries resolve to "nothing found", which is the point
of them). The verifier is built with offline=True, so a cache miss is a hard
error and nothing can reach the network.

  expected verdict        n   entries
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------
  MATCH                   5   entry-02, 07, 13, 15, 19
  MATCH_WITH_VARIANTS     5   entry-03, 08, 12, 16, 23
  ORDER_DIFFERS           3   entry-05, 11, 18
  TRUNCATED               4   entry-06, 09, 20, 25
  PARTIAL_OVERLAP         3   entry-01, 14, 24
  DISJOINT                5   entry-04, 10, 17, 21, 22
  UNVERIFIABLE            2   entry-26, 27
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------
  7 verdicts             27

What each group covers:

  entry-01   the real chimeric citation recorded on 29 Oct 2026: the true
             author list of arXiv 2507.01413 is Kushal Agrawal, Verona Teo,
             Juan J. Vazquez, Sudarsh Kunnavakkam, Vishak Srikanth and Andy
             Liu, and the fabricated list keeps Agrawal and Liu while
             replacing the other four with five real researchers who had
             nothing to do with the work.
  entry-02   the same entry with its true author list.
  entry-03   the same true list abbreviated to initials.
  entry-04   a wholly fabricated author list on the same real identifier.
  entry-05   the true list with the last author moved to the front.
  entry-06   the true list cut short with "and others".
  entry-07   AlphaGo, the full deposited list including a Dutch particle
             surname.
  entry-08   the same correct list with that one name restyled as
             "Driessche, George van den".
  entry-12   AlphaFold, the full list with the one accented name folded to
             ASCII.
  entry-13   the same list with that name written in LaTeX accent commands.
  entry-16   ResNet with all four names written family-name-first.
  entry-19   GW150914 cited by its 1012-author consortium name alone,
             brace-protected so BibTeX keeps it whole.
  entry-20   GW150914 cited as the first three authors plus "and others".
  entry-22   GW150914 attributed to the wrong consortium (ATLAS).
  entry-23   Attention Is All You Need with no identifier, so the record has
             to be found by bibliographic search.
  entry-24   a Qwen2.5 citation with no identifier, resolved through the
             OpenAlex title search, with one invented author in the list.
  entry-26   a real-looking ACM DOI that is in none of the fixtures.
  entry-27   no identifier and a title no recorded search covers.

Each entry carries a "label_basis" that says why the expected verdict is what
it is, and a "requires_cache" naming the fixture in
tests/fixtures/cache/INDEX.json that must be present for it to resolve.


6. WHAT THIS SET DOES NOT MEASURE
---------------------------------

Stated so that nobody quotes the numbers for more than they are worth.

  * It is not a random sample of anything. It is a hand-built set weighted
    towards the hard cases, so the accuracy figure is not an estimate of
    accuracy on a random bibliography. On an ordinary bibliography the tool
    will score much higher, because most entries are easy.
  * 154 pairs and 27 entries are small. A single row moves pair accuracy by
    0.65 of a percentage point and entry accuracy by 3.7.
  * Author-list order beyond a single permutation, non-Latin scripts other
    than Han, and right-to-left scripts are not covered.
  * The online paths are not exercised at all. Everything here runs against
    recorded responses, so provider ranking, rate limiting and live failure
    handling are outside the measurement.
  * Two of the three categories with a perfect score (exact, middle_name)
    have no negatives in them by construction, so their accuracy figure
    carries no information about false positives.
